lesson.title: The Short List of Atoms That Build Every Living Thing
lesson.summary: This section introduces the handful of chemical elements, especially carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur, that make up the overwhelming majority of living matter, and explains why carbon's atomic structure makes it uniquely suited to building life's molecules.
lesson.body:
Living organisms are built almost entirely from a strikingly short list of chemical elements, even though the periodic table contains over a hundred. Four elements, carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen, make up roughly ninety six percent of the mass of a typical living cell. Phosphorus and sulfur bring the total to about ninety nine percent when included, giving biologists a convenient shorthand for life's core elements: C, H, O, N, P, S. A handful of additional elements, including calcium, potassium, sodium, chlorine, magnesium, and iron, appear in smaller but still essential amounts, often playing specific roles such as forming bone mineral, carrying electrical signals across nerve cells, or sitting at the center of the oxygen carrying heme group in hemoglobin. Beyond these, trace elements like zinc, copper, and iodine are needed in tiny quantities, frequently as helpers bound to particular proteins.

Why this particular set of elements, rather than some other combination drawn from the periodic table? The answer traces back to atomic structure, specifically the number and arrangement of electrons in an atom's outermost, or valence, shell, which determines how many bonds an atom can form and with what geometry. Carbon has four valence electrons, which means it can form four covalent bonds simultaneously. This is the single most important fact in all of biological chemistry, because it lets carbon act as a stable scaffold, bonding to other carbon atoms to build chains and rings while still having bonds left over to attach hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and other groups. No other biologically abundant element matches this combination of bonding capacity and stability. Silicon, directly below carbon in the same column of the periodic table, also has four valence electrons and can theoretically form similar bonds, but silicon based molecules are far less stable under the conditions found in living cells, which is part of why life on Earth is carbon based rather than silicon based.

Hydrogen, with a single valence electron, forms one bond at a time and is the smallest and most abundant atom by number in biological molecules, frequently filling out the remaining bonding positions on a carbon skeleton. Oxygen, with six valence electrons, typically forms two bonds and pulls shared electrons toward itself strongly, a property called electronegativity that becomes central once we discuss chemical bonds and water polarity later in this chapter. Nitrogen, with five valence electrons, usually forms three bonds and is a defining component of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and of the nitrogenous bases that spell out genetic information in DNA and RNA. Phosphorus, often forming four bonds, is the backbone atom in the phosphate groups that link nucleotides together in DNA and RNA and that store retrievable chemical energy in molecules like ATP. Sulfur appears in two of the twenty amino acids and helps stabilize protein shape through disulfide bonds.

Understanding which elements make up living matter, and why their valence electron counts make them suited to the job, sets up everything that follows in this chapter. The next sections examine exactly how these atoms connect to one another, through ionic bonds, covalent bonds, hydrogen bonds, and van der Waals forces, each of which depends directly on the number of valence electrons an atom has available and how strongly it attracts those electrons, the same atomic structure concepts introduced here.
